articles.description: On the frontlines of healthcare, and the strategy table. A cool July afternoon at the Wellcome Collection with the Zimbabwean-British doctor and founder of the women's-health venture Glacie Health, on calling, on education as a form of medicine, and on carrying what the West knows back home to the women who need it.

articles.title: Zimbabwe's tobacco anchor in Britain holds at £129m
articles.description: Of every £100 of goods Zimbabwe sells to Britain, £96 is tobacco or beverages. While the wider UK–Zimbabwe trade relationship softened in the year to December 2025, Zimbabwean tobacco held its grip, and the IMF projects Zimbabwean GDP growth of 7.5% in 2025 and 5.0% in 2026. The product that built Zimbabwe's name as an exporter is still doing the work.

more.title: The Apple of haircare gets its German cheque
more.description: Ruka, the London-based textured-hair company founded by Zimbabwean entrepreneur Varaidzo Tendai Moyo and her co-founder Ugorji Agbai, has closed a $4.5m round co-led by Henkel Ventures and Freedom Trail Capital. The deal, which takes lifetime funding to roughly $10m and brings one of the world's largest consumer-goods groups onto the cap table, is the most meaningful endorsement yet of a Zimbabwean diaspora-founded brand.

more.title: Pardon Mapondera: gone but not forgotten at Venice
more.description: The fifth and final piece in our series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Pardon Mapondera, the artist whose practice the room finally arranges itself around, treats discarded plastic and glass jars not as ecological signal but as ritual matter, and produces, in the process, the most quietly devotional installation in the Biennale this year.

more.title: Gideon Gomo: from stone to bronze, the ancestral algorithm at Venice
more.description: The fourth in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Gideon Gomo's first sustained body of bronze work, paired with discarded vehicle number plates and Zimbabwean springstone, is the move of a sculptor at full maturity rethinking the material vocabulary of his country's most internationally legible art form.

more.title: Shumba Maasai in Venice
more.description: At the 61st Biennale, the Zimbabwean artist's day-long procession through the city's campi, performed under the borrowed authority of a Murehwa chief, restages the social-sculpture lineage of Joseph Beuys for a contemporary African discursive practice.

more.title: Franklyn Dzingai: family albums and the neural commons at Venice
more.description: The third in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Franklyn Dzingai's reductive cardboard prints, built from the family album, the magazine clipping, the back-room studio photographs of mid-century Zimbabwe, turn out, on close looking, to be the most precisely engineered work in the room.

more.title: Felix Shumba: charcoal and the practice of disappearance at Venice
more.description: The second in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Felix Shumba's six-metre charcoal wall and his Telephone Reader series anchor a body of work that argues drawing is not the act of capturing the seen, but the act of staying present to what is on its way out of sight.

more.title: UK services share in Zimbabwe rises to 8.2%
more.description: The headline UK services trade with Zimbabwe softened year on year. The structural number underneath it tells the better story: Britain's share of all services Zimbabwe imports rose 2.4 percentage points to 8.2%, the highest measured level in years. As Zimbabwean buyers re-rate their global supplier mix, the UK is taking a bigger slice of the country's services demand.

more.title: Zimbabwe's demand lifts British exports by 14.6%
more.description: The Zimbabwean economy is in its strongest stretch in years: 7.5% GDP growth in 2025, a projected 5% in 2026, and that growth is pulling demand for cars, commercial vehicles, medicines and industrial machinery in with it. UK goods exports to Zimbabwe rose 14.6% on the year, the strongest line in an otherwise soft bilateral picture for Britain.

more.title: NSSA moves to extend social security to informal workers
more.description: Theseus Mauruki Shambare in VICTORIA FALLS THE National Social Security Authority (NSSA) is on the verge of piloting a new social security scheme targeting workers in Zimbabwe’s informal economy, as the Tripartite Negotiating Forum (TNF) Global Summit enters its second day in Victoria Falls. The proposed scheme is part of wider discussions at the summit on employment creation, social protection and building an inclusive global economy capable of responding to changing labour-market realities. NSSA Director of Social Security and Benefits, Actuarial and Schemes Development, Mr Shepherd Muperi, said the authority had undertaken extensive research to develop a social security programme suited to the circumstances of informal economy workers. The initiative is being developed with the International Labour Organisation (ILO), with stakeholder consultations having been conducted to determine the priorities of informal workers and ensure that the scheme is affordable and sustainable. “As we speak, we are at the verge of almost implementing or piloting a specific, appropriate and suitable social security scheme for workers in the informal economy,” Mr Muperi said. The proposed expansion comes against a backdrop of a labour market in which a significant proportion of workers operate outside conventional formal employment arrangements, limiting their access to social protection schemes traditionally based on employer-employee relationships. Mr Muperi said existing schemes had largely been designed around formal employment, stable salaries and identifiable employers, making them less suited to informal workers and emerging forms of employment such as platform work. “We appreciate that they may not be able to join the formal schemes that we have that are based on employer-employee relationships, because, traditionally, these social security schemes were designed for employment-based where there is employer and employee and stable salaries,” he said. The proposed scheme will seek to incorporate incentives that respond to the practical challenges facing informal businesses and workers. Mr Muperi said these could include access to decent workspaces and affordable funding to help informal businesses develop and grow. “The challenge is that people want informal economy workers to contribute even towards taxes, but the focus should be more on: how are we supporting them to develop their business, to grow them?” he said. He said informal workers had also been involved in the design process, helping NSSA identify the social risks and benefits they considered priorities. “The design is coming from with them, and they have expressed their priority needs in terms of all the life risks to say: this is what we want covered,” Mr Muperi said. The issue of extending social protection to workers outside the formal economy also featured prominently in the summit’s discussions on the future of decent work. Director of the ILO Country Office for Zimbabwe and Namibia, Ms Philile Ntombikayise Masuku, said Zimbabwe should move towards implementing its recently endorsed formalisation strategy while progressively extending social protection to informal and platform workers. “We need to commit to making sure that it is implemented and also commit to the gradual extension of social protection to informal workers and also the workers in the platform economy,” she said. Mr Muperi said social security could also play a role in mobilising domestic resources for national development, with pooled funds potentially supporting infrastructure and productive investments. He cited dams, roads, energy projects and industry as areas where social security funds could contribute to development while supporting economic activity and employment creation. “Social security is acknowledged worldwide as a very important vehicle for mobilizing local resources for national development,” he said. As the TNF Global Summit continues, the proposed NSSA scheme adds a practical dimension to the broader call for social protection to reach workers across Zimbabwe’s changing labour market, including those outside traditional formal employment.

more.title: ‘Give us first preference’: Ngozi mine residents appeal to Geo Pomona
more.description: Sikhumbuzo Moyo smoyo@chronicle.co.zw RESIDENTS living at Richmond Landfill, popularly known as Ngozi Mine, have appealed to Geo Pomona Waste Management to prioritise them for employment when the company takes over waste recycling operations at the site. The residents made the appeal during a site visit by the Zimbabwe National Organisation of Associations and Residents Trusts (ZNOART), saying they had no objection to Geo Pomona taking over the recycling operations but wanted to benefit through employment opportunities. Some residents have lived at the landfill for decades and depend on waste picking for their livelihoods. Ms Limukani Sibanda, who said she had lived at the site since 1994, said residents had gained extensive experience in handling and sorting waste. “I have been living here since 1994. I know no other home than this place. We have heard that a company called Geo Pomona is coming to take over the place, so our appeal to them is that they prioritise us when employing. We have the experience of picking waste,” she said. Ms Sibanda also raised concerns over a long-standing housing promise by the Bulawayo City Council, saying residents had been placed on a waiting list for housing but had yet to receive stands. She said residents were asked to pay US$50 in 2013 and were subsequently allocated stand numbers, which they have continued to renew annually. “We were asked to deposit US$50 in 2013 and we were given stand numbers. Every year we are renewing with council, but our stands have not come out,” said Ms Sibanda. Another resident, Mr Nicholas Mpala, welcomed the proposed involvement of Geo Pomona but echoed the call for locals to be given first preference for jobs. “We welcome this development, but our appeal is to be given first priority in terms of employment,” he said. The residents’ concerns come as authorities seek to address challenges at the Richmond Landfill, including waste management and the impact of activities at the site on surrounding communities.
